description_full: Ryerson Holding Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, processes and distributes industrial metals in the United States and internationally. It offers a line of products in carbon steel, stainless steel, alloy steels, and aluminum, as well as nickel and red metals in various shapes and forms, including coils, sheets, rounds, hexagons, square and flat bars, plates, structural, and tubing. The company also provides processing services. It serves commercial transportation, fabrication and welding, machinery and equipment, consumer products, heavy equipment, climate, power, and machine shop industries. Ryerson Holding Corporation was founded in 1842 and is headquartered in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Ryerson Holding Corporation is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.5B market cap on $4.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 20% against a 10% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The business throws off $36M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin -0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 6.3% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
